## Other cable modems worth considering

If you want to save some money and don’t plan on upgrading to a multi-gig internet plan: The Arris SURFboard SB8200 is a good alternative to our pick that may save you a few dollars. It is DOCSIS 3.1 certified, and it appears on all the approved modem lists we track. It has a two-year warranty and is worth considering if you find it priced $30 to $50 below the S33. It has Gigabit Ethernet ports instead of a 2.5 GbE port, but it’s entirely sufficient if you subscribe to a midtier (300 to 1,000 Mbps) plan. [...] The Arris SURFboard SB6183 was a pick in 2017, and we reevaluated it against the Netgear CM500 since that model is similar in specs and price. However, the SB6183 has a note on Cox’s approved modems list to contact Cox to discuss upgrade options; that note does not bode well for the SB6183’s longevity. We also evaluated the Arris SURFboard SB6190 and Netgear CM700 as cheaper alternatives to our pick, but neither DOCSIS 3.0 modem had full 1 Gbps support from most ISPs.

results.title: Modem vs router: What is the difference, and do you need both? | Verizon
results.content:
Equally important is to consider the types of internet connections you have and the speed of your internet service. If you have a high-speed fiber-optic connection, you may need a newer modem-router combo that can handle that type of connection. On the other hand, if you only have a slow DSL connection, and you don’t need to connect wirelessly, a standalone modem may be all you need.

Here’s the rundown of each type of modem and router so you can make a decision.

### Singular modem

On one hand, a standalone modem is simple to set up and use. Typically, you’ll only need an Ethernet cable to connect to the modem and get internet, regardless of whether it’s dial-up, DSL or cable. [...] On the other hand, this simple set-up is a limitation, as you may not want to deal with an Ethernet cable, and you can only connect one device to the modem’s single Ethernet port. Worse yet, a modem doesn’t come with any built-in security and privacy features, and you may need to replace it if your ISP upgrades its equipment.

### Separate modem and router

If you opt for a separate modem and router, you’ll get a more secure connection than a modem alone can offer. You’ll be able to connect a variety of devices, and if the router is wireless, you can do so without cables. The router should also offer more security features than a standalone modem would. [...] Wireless routers: A wireless router connects to a modem via an Ethernet cable. This transmits data by converting binary code into radio waves. Signals are broadcast wirelessly using antennas. Wireless routers don't create LANs; instead, they establish WLANs that connect several wireless devices.
 Wired routers: A wired router connects to a modem using an Ethernet connection. It then uses other cables to link the network's devices to one another and connect them to the internet.

Each type of router has its advantages and disadvantages. For example, wireless routers are generally easier to set up and use, but wired routers can provide a more secure connection.

## Do I need a modem and a router?

results.title: Modems vs. Routers
results.content:
For modems: It’s important to pick one that works with your internet type—DSL, cable, or fiber—to ensure compatibility.
 For routers: Think about what features you need based on your home’s activities, like streaming movies, online gaming, or working from home. Some routers offer faster speeds, wider coverage, and added security, which can be a game-changer for busy households.

When it comes to renting vs. buying a modem-router combo, each option has its pros and cons. Renting from your ISP is easy and guarantees compatibility, but the costs can add up over time. Buying can save money in the long run and give you more control over your setup, but it might require a bit of technical know-how to manage. [...] Match your internet service: Make sure the modem you choose matches the type of internet service you have—whether it’s DSL, cable, or fiber. For example, a cable modem typically won’t work with a fiber connection, as a fiber connection requires an ONT.
 Look for speed support: Speed support is another important factor to think about. Choose a modem that matches your internet plan's speed tier. For high-speed internet or gigabit plans, we recommend a DOCSIS 3.1 modem because it delivers faster, more stable connections compared to DOCSIS 3.0. [...] Without a modem, you wouldn’t have direct access to the internet. It’s the essential piece that connects your home to your ISP. Depending on the internet connection type—whether DSL, cable, or fiber—the modem will differ. For example, our Kinetic Gateways are designed for different connections, ensuring reliable internet access tailored to our specific internet service options.

### What is a router used for?

While a modem connects your home to the internet, a router manages and sends that internet signal to multiple devices. It acts as the air traffic controller of your network, ensuring data flows smoothly to and from your connected devices.
